intro: Nine matriculation-exam-style problems bring together the photons, atoms, nuclei and radiation of the lesson. Solve them as in the exam: name the phenomenon and the model and justify why the model fits the situation, solve for the quantity asked before substituting numbers, and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the marking scheme only when your solution is ready. Problem 7 is an applied source-based problem; its source opens from the link in the problem. Problems 8 and 9 work with a graph.

tasks.title: Caesium in forest mushrooms
tasks.source_note: The activity concentrations of the mushrooms are an invented example. The half-life of caesium-137, the gamma photon energy $662\,\text{keV}$ and the adult dose coefficient $1.3 \cdot 10^{-8}\,\tfrac{\text{Sv}}{\text{Bq}}$ are real values.
tasks.text:
The fallout of the Chernobyl accident left caesium-137 in Finnish forests, and it accumulates especially in mushrooms. Caesium-137 decays by beta minus decay into barium-137m, which is an excited nucleus of barium. It returns to the ground state by emitting a gamma photon whose energy is $662\,\text{keV}$. In a forest area in the Häme region, the caesium-137 concentration of funnel chanterelles was measured in 1990 as $2400\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{kg}}$ fresh weight.

- atomic number of caesium $55$, of barium $56$
- half-life of caesium-137 $30.1\,\text{a}$, $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$
- dose coefficient: one ingested becquerel of caesium-137 gives an adult an effective dose of $1.3 \cdot 10^{-8}\,\text{Sv}$
- the average effective dose of a person in Finland is about $5.9\,\text{mSv}$ per year
- assume that caesium leaves the mushrooms only by decaying

parts.text: Write the equations of the decay of caesium-137 and the de-excitation of barium-137m. How large is the wavelength of the gamma photon?
hints: In beta minus decay a neutron of the nucleus turns into a proton. Which numbers of the nucleus change, which stay the same, and what does the nucleus emit?
On both sides of the arrow the sum of the mass numbers and the sum of the charge numbers must be equal. The photon energy and the wavelength are related: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.
Convert the energy to joules first: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Then solve the wavelength $\lambda$ and convert it to picometres, $1\,\text{pm} = 10^{-12}\,\text{m}$.

criteria.text: Writes ${}^{137}_{55}\text{Cs} \to {}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba}^{\ast} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} + \bar{\nu}$ and ${}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba}^{\ast} \to {}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba} + \gamma$ so that the mass number and the charge number are conserved.

parts.text: How large is the caesium-137 concentration of the same mushrooms in 2026?
hints: What happens to each caesium nucleus as time passes, and do new nuclei appear? How many half-lives have passed from 1990 to 2026?

The activity halves in every half-life:
$$
A = A_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}
$$
The time is $t = 2026 - 1990$ years, and the half-life is in the same unit, so no conversion is needed. Calculate the ratio $t/T_{1/2}$ first and substitute it into the exponent.

criteria.text: Justifies that the activity decreases according to the decay law, because each nucleus decays with the same probability and no new caesium comes in.

parts.text: During 2026 a mushroom picker eats $5.0\,\text{kg}$ of such mushrooms. How large an effective dose does the picker get from the mushrooms? Compare the dose with the average annual dose of a person in Finland.
hints: How many becquerels does the mushroom picker eat in total? What does the dose coefficient tell?

The activity eaten is the concentration times the mass, and the dose follows from the dose coefficient:
$$
H = A_m \cdot m \cdot k_\text{dose}
$$

Use the concentration of part b. Calculate the dose in sieverts and convert it to millisieverts, $1\,\text{Sv} = 1000\,\text{mSv}$. Compare it with the average annual dose $5.9\,\text{mSv}$ as a fraction.

criteria.detail: ingested activity $A m$ and dose $H_\text{E} = A m \cdot k$, where $k$ is the dose coefficient
About $1\,\%$ of the average $5.9\,\text{mSv}$, so the share of the mushrooms is small.

parts.text: How many caesium-137 nuclei are there in one kilogram of mushrooms in 2026, and how large is their mass? The mass of a caesium-137 atom is $137\,\text{u}$, $1\,\text{u} = 1.66 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$.
hints: The activity tells the number of decays per second. How are the activity, the decay constant and the number of nuclei related?

The activity and the decay constant:
$$
A = \lambda N, \quad \lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}
$$
Solve the number of nuclei $N$ from these.
Convert the half-life to seconds: $30.1\,\text{a} = 30.1 \cdot 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$. The mass is the product $m = N\,m_\text{a}$, where $m_\text{a} = 137\,\text{u}$ is the mass of one atom.

criteria.detail: $A = \lambda N$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$, so $N = \dfrac{A T_{1/2}}{\ln 2}$; mass $m = N \cdot 137\,\text{u}$

tasks.title: Hydrogen lines in a distant galaxy
tasks.source_note: The galaxy and the wavelength of its spectrum are an invented example. The laboratory values $656.3\,\text{nm}$ and $486.1\,\text{nm}$ of the hydrogen lines are real.
tasks.text:
On an upper secondary astronomy course, students study the spectrum of a distant galaxy measured with the spectrograph of a telescope. The spectrum has dark lines, and the strongest of them is identified as the red line of hydrogen.

- energy levels of the hydrogen atom $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
- wavelength of the red line of hydrogen in the laboratory $656.3\,\text{nm}$ and of the cyan line $486.1\,\text{nm}$
- in the spectrum of the galaxy the red line is at the wavelength $671.8\,\text{nm}$
- Hubble constant $H_0 = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, speed of light $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$

parts.text: The red line of hydrogen arises in the transition from level $3$ to level $2$. Calculate the wavelength of the line from the levels.
hints: What does an atom emit when an electron moves from a higher level to a lower one? Where does the energy of the photon come from?
The energy of the photon is the difference of the energies of the levels, $E_\text{f} = E_3 - E_2$, and the energy and the wavelength of a photon are related: $E_\text{f} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

Calculate the energies of the levels and their difference in electronvolts. Convert the difference to joules, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$, before you solve the wavelength $\lambda$.

criteria.text: Justifies that the photon energy is the difference of the levels $E_3 - E_2$, because energy is conserved in the transition.

parts.text: At what speed is the galaxy receding from us, and how far away is it?
hints: Compare the observed wavelength with the laboratory value. Which quantity tells how much the wavelength has changed relative to the original, and how is it related to the motion of the galaxy?

The redshift $z$, the recession speed for a small $z$ and Hubble's law:
$$
\begin{aligned}z &= \dfrac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0} \\ v &= cz \\ v &= H_0\,d\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the redshift $z$ first from the difference of the wavelengths, divided by the laboratory value. Use the speed of light in $\text{km/s}$ so that the speed comes out in $\text{km/s}$. Finally solve the distance $d$.

criteria.text: Justifies that the line has shifted to longer wavelengths because the galaxy recedes as space expands, and that the redshift is small, so $v = cz$ holds.

criteria.detail: $v \approx 7.1 \cdot 10^{3}\,\text{km/s}$ and $d \approx 100\,\text{Mpc}$, two significant figures like the Hubble constant

parts.text: At what wavelength does the cyan line of hydrogen appear in the spectrum of the galaxy?
hints: Which quantity describes how much the wavelength has stretched? Does it depend on which line of the spectrum you look at?
The redshift is $z = \dfrac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}$. Use the $z$ of part b and solve the observed wavelength $\lambda$ from the equation.
The laboratory value of the cyan line is $486.1\,\text{nm}$. The wavelength stays in nanometres, so no conversion is needed.

criteria.text: Justifies that the redshift $z$ is the same for every line of the spectrum.

parts.text: Explain why the hydrogen lines in the spectrum of the galaxy are dark and not bright.
hints: What is the spectrum of the light before it passes through the outer gas layers of a star? What happens to the light in the gas layer?
Think about which photon a hydrogen atom can absorb. Which energy is the position of the line in the spectrum related to (part a)?
The atom emits the energy it absorbed again later. In which directions? Compare how much light reaches us at the line and at the neighbouring wavelengths.

criteria.text: Explains that the hot surface of the stars emits a continuous spectrum, and the outermost gas layers of the stars lie between it and the observer.
Explains that hydrogen atoms absorb only photons whose energy is exactly the difference of levels, and re-emit the energy in all directions.

criteria.detail: The light coming towards the observer lacks exactly the wavelengths of hydrogen, so the lines are darker than their surroundings.

tasks.title: The photoelectric effect and the Planck constant
tasks.source_note: The voltages have been calculated from the photoelectric equation, and variation like that of measurements has been added to them.
tasks.text:
In a physics lab a photocell whose cathode is potassium is studied. When the cathode is lit, electrons leave it and travel through a vacuum to the anode, and a photocurrent flows in the circuit. A voltage that slows the electrons down is connected between the anode and the cathode: the anode is more negative than the cathode. The voltage is increased until the photocurrent just stops. This voltage is called the stopping voltage $U$. The cathode was lit in turn with different wavelengths using an LED light source and filters.

| $\lambda\ (\text{nm})$ | $U\ (\text{V})$ |
|---|---|
| $365$ | $1.15$ |
| $405$ | $0.80$ |
| $436$ | $0.61$ |
| $470$ | $0.38$ |
| $505$ | $0.21$ |
| $590$ | no current |

- $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$

parts.text: Present the stopping voltage as a function of the frequency of the light as a graph.
hints: The table gives wavelengths, but the graph must show the frequency. What about the last row: what can you say about the stopping voltage when no current flows?
The frequency follows from the wavelength: $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}$. The stopping voltage $U$ is on the vertical axis and the frequency $f$ on the horizontal axis.

Convert the wavelength to metres, for example $365\,\text{nm} = 365 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$. Use $10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ as the unit of the horizontal axis and choose the scale so that the points fill the graph.

criteria.detail: $f\ (10^{14}\,\text{Hz})$ on the horizontal axis, $U\ (\text{V})$ on the vertical axis; axes named and units marked.

criteria.text: Does not plot a point for the wavelength $590\,\text{nm}$, because no photocurrent arises there, and does not join the points into a broken line.

parts.text: Justify why a straight line fits the points, and fit a straight line to the points. Extend the line so that it crosses both axes.
hints: When the photocurrent just stops, what has happened to the kinetic energy of the fastest electron in the electric field? Which energy has been conserved?

Combine two equations: the photoelectric equation, where the photon energy $hf$ is shared between the work function $W$ and the kinetic energy, and the condition of the stopping voltage. What kind of function is $U$ of the frequency $f$?
Draw the line through the points so that there are points on both sides of it. Extend the line with a dashed line across the horizontal axis and up to the vertical axis, where $f = 0$.

criteria.text: Justifies with conservation of energy: the kinetic energy $E_\text{k,max}$ of the fastest electron is used up entirely in the braking work done by the electric field, so $eU = E_\text{k,max}$.
Combines this with the photoelectric equation: $eU = hf - W$, so $U = \dfrac{h}{e}\,f - \dfrac{W}{e}$ is the equation of a straight line.

criteria.detail: One straight line between the points, extended as a dashed line to the vertical axis and to the horizontal axis.

parts.text: Determine the Planck constant from the graph. Compare the result with the value $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$.
hints: Look at the equation of part b, where $U$ is a function of the frequency. Which of its coefficients contains the Planck constant?
The slope of the line is calculated from two points read on the line: $k = \dfrac{\Delta U}{\Delta f}$. Combine it with the equation of part b and solve $h$.

Read two points far apart on the fitted line, not from the measured points. Unit: $1\,\text{C} \cdot 1\,\text{V} \cdot 1\,\text{s} = 1\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$. Finally calculate by how many per cent the result differs from the reference value.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(0;\ -2.24\,\text{V})$ and $(8.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 1.06\,\text{V})$: $k \approx 4.13 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$

criteria.text: Interprets the slope: $k = \dfrac{h}{e}$.

criteria.detail: Compares the difference with the table value $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$ and assesses whether it is within the reading accuracy of the graph.

parts.text: Determine from the graph the work function of potassium in electronvolts and the threshold frequency. Explain why no photocurrent arises at the wavelength $590\,\text{nm}$, and whether the situation would change if there were ten times more $590\,\text{nm}$ light.
hints: What does the intercept of the line with the vertical axis tell, and what does its intercept with the horizontal axis tell? What is $U$ at the threshold frequency?
The constant term is $-\dfrac{W}{e}$, and at the threshold frequency the energy of the photon is just enough for the work function: $hf_0 = W$.

Calculate the frequency of the $590\,\text{nm}$ light, $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}$, and compare it with the threshold frequency. Then think what ten times more intensity changes: the energy of one photon or the number of photons?

criteria.detail: The line crosses the vertical axis at $-\tfrac{W}{e} \approx -2.24\,\text{V}$ and the horizontal axis at $f_0 \approx 5.43 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

criteria.text: Calculates that the frequency $5.08 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ of $590\,\text{nm}$ is smaller than the threshold frequency, that is, the photon energy $2.10\,\text{eV}$ is smaller than the work function.

criteria.detail: Brighter light brings more photons but not more energetic ones, so still no electrons leave.

tasks.title: Radon at the housing company meeting
tasks.source_note: The meeting and the measurement result are an invented example. The reference level $300\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$ for the radon concentration of dwellings follows the Finnish Radiation Act.
tasks.text:
In the flats of a terraced-house company in Hyvinkää, the radon concentration was measured in winter for two months. The result of one flat was $450\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$. At the residents' meeting three claims were made.

1. “The alpha radiation of radon is stopped by paper and by the surface of the skin, so it cannot be dangerous.”
2. “The half-life of radon is only $3.8$ days. If we keep the windows tightly shut for a month, the radon will disappear by itself.”
3. “The neighbour had a dental X-ray. Now she is radioactive too, so the children should not be near her.”

The reference level for the radon concentration of dwellings is $300\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$. Radon-222 forms from radium in the decay series of uranium in the soil and bedrock.

parts.text: Assess claim 1. Explain how radon causes a radiation dose.
hints: Is the justification of the claim correct when the radiation source is outside the body? How does radon get into the human body?
Think about the properties of an alpha particle: mass, charge and how densely it ionises. Where does its energy go when the particle stops inside the body?
The dose also depends on the radiation weighting factor. What is the weighting factor of alpha radiation compared with gamma and beta radiation, and what does it tell about the equivalent dose?

criteria.text: States that alpha radiation does not penetrate the skin, so external alpha radiation is not dangerous; that part of the claim's justification is true.
Explains that radon and its decay products are breathed into the lungs, where the alpha radiation hits the cells of the lungs directly.
Justifies the danger: an alpha particle ionises densely and gives up its energy over a distance of a few cells, and its weighting factor is $20$.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: radon is the largest source of radiation dose for people in Finland, and $450\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$ is $1.5$ times the reference level, so the concentration should be reduced.

parts.text: Assess claim 2. According to the model, what fraction of the radon nuclei in the room is still undecayed after a month, and does the radon still disappear from the flat?
hints: What fraction of the nuclei is left after a given number of half-lives? Does the calculation also cover nuclei that enter the room later?

The fraction left follows the law of radioactive decay:
$$
\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}
$$

A month is about $30\,\text{d}$ and the half-life is $3.8\,\text{d}$. First calculate how many half-lives a month contains. Then think where the radon comes from in the first place and how it gets into the flat.

criteria.detail: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{30 : 3.8} \approx 0.004$, that is about $0.4\,\%$ of the original radon nuclei

criteria.text: States that the calculation holds only for the nuclei that were in the room at the start.
Explains that the uranium decay series in the soil produces radon all the time, and it flows in through cracks in the foundations when the pressure indoors is lower.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: when the windows and ventilation are closed, as much new radon comes in as before but less of it leaves, so the concentration increases. The concentration is reduced by ventilation and by sealing the structures.

parts.text: Assess claim 3.
hints: What does ionising radiation do to tissue during the imaging? What happens after the X-ray machine has been switched off?
Separate radioactivity (a property of unstable nuclei) from the ionisation caused by radiation (the electrons of atoms). Which one does an X-ray photon affect?
What can an X-ray photon with an energy of about $60\,\text{keV}$ do to an atom, and what to a nucleus? Then think when a person really is a radiation source, for example in an isotope examination.

criteria.text: Explains that X-rays are photon radiation that either passes through the tissue or is absorbed and ionises atoms during the imaging.
Justifies that radioactivity is a property of unstable nuclei, and the energy of an X-ray photon, about $60\,\text{keV}$, ionises atoms but does not change nuclei.
Distinguishes external exposure from radioactive material entering the body: only the latter makes a person a radiation source, as a tracer of a nuclear medicine examination does for a short time.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: when the X-ray unit switches off, there is no radiation any more, and no radiation comes from the neighbour to the children.

tasks.title: The half-life of barium-137m
tasks.source_note: The report and the measurements are an invented example. The readings have been calculated with a half-life of $153\,\text{s}$ and a background of $5$ counts in $10\,\text{s}$, and variation like the randomness of decay has been added to them.
tasks.text:
A group of students measured the half-life of barium-137m. The barium solution was eluted from an isotope generator into a sample dish, and the dish was placed under a GM tube. The counts were recorded in $10\,\text{s}$ periods every $30\,\text{s}$. Before the measurement the background radiation was measured once for $10\,\text{s}$, giving $5$ counts.

| $t\ (\text{s})$ | counts $/\ 10\,\text{s}$ |
|---|---|
| $0$ | $398$ |
| $30$ | $361$ |
| $60$ | $304$ |
| $90$ | $276$ |
| $120$ | $231$ |
| $150$ | $212$ |
| $180$ | $188$ |
| $210$ | $163$ |
| $240$ | $136$ |
| $270$ | $127$ |
| $300$ | $104$ |

The group's conclusion: “At the start there were $398$ counts, and half of that, $199$, was reached at about $166\,\text{s}$. So the half-life is $166\,\text{s}$, which is $8\,\%$ more than the book value $153\,\text{s}$. The difference is because the solution stood in the dish for about a minute before the measurement, so the remaining nuclei were older and decayed more slowly. The background did not need to be subtracted, because it was only $5$ counts.”

parts.text: Determine the half-life from the data, taking the background radiation into account.
hints: The GM tube also counts the pulses of the background radiation. What must you do to every reading before you look for the half-life?

The pulse count of the sample follows the law of radioactive decay, so $\ln N$ is a straight line of time. The half-life follows from the decay constant:
$$
N = N_0\,e^{-\lambda t}, \quad T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
$$

Calculate $\ln N$ for every reading after the background has been subtracted and plot the points $(t,\ \ln N)$. The slope of the line is $-\lambda$. Fit the line to all the points, not only to the first and the last.

criteria.text: Subtracts the background from each of the $11$ readings before calculating: $393$ at the start and $99$ at the end, counts in $10\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $\ln N = \ln N_0 - \lambda t$, so the slope of the line $(t,\ \ln N)$ is $k = -\lambda$ and $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{-k}$; a fit to all the points. The two-point calculation $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{t \ln 2}{\ln (N_0 : N)}$ is also accepted
$k \approx -4.53 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{s}}$ and $T_{1/2} \approx 153\,\text{s}$; about $151\,\text{s}$ with the two-point calculation
The result is within a few per cent of the book value $153\,\text{s}$.

parts.text: Assess the group's conclusion.
hints: Check each part of the group's reasoning separately: reading the half-life, handling the background and the explanation. Which of them hold?
Think whether a nucleus has an age: does the decay probability of one barium-137m nucleus depend on how long it has existed?

Compare the background, $5$ pulses in $10\,\text{s}$, with the first reading $398$ and the last reading $104$. Is the background negligible at every moment of the measurement? Also think what one pair of points tells about random variation.

criteria.text: States that the explanation is wrong: a nucleus has no age, but every barium-137m nucleus has the same decay probability per second, so standing does not change the half-life.

criteria.detail: The half-life was read from a single reading and by interpolating between two points, so the random variation of decay in one reading affects it directly.
States that the background should have been subtracted: a background measured once is uncertain, and its share grows at the end: $5$ counts is about $5\,\%$ of the reading $104$.
The difference $166\,\text{s}$ versus $153\,\text{s}$ comes from the way of measuring and reading, not from the sample; the whole data set gives about $151$–$153\,\text{s}$.

parts.text: Plan how the measurement and the processing of the results can be improved.
hints: What in the measurement and in the processing of the results caused the most uncertainty or error? How could each problem be corrected?
Divide the improvements into two groups: what is measured differently and how the results are processed. Which has the larger effect on the result?
When the pulse count is small, the random variation is large in proportion. In which two ways can its effect be reduced? How can you see how large the spread of the result is?

criteria.text: Measures the background for a long time, for example $10\,\text{min}$, before or after the measurement and subtracts it from each reading in the same unit.
Uses all the measurement points: fits the model $y = A\,e^{-Ct} + B$ to the points, or draws a graph and determines the half-life from the fitted curve.
Lengthens the counting time or repeats the whole measurement with a new sample and compares the results, so that the random variation decreases and the spread can be seen.

criteria.detail: Estimates the uncertainty of the result from the spread of the repeats or with the fit before comparing it with the book value.

tasks.title: Electricity from a nuclear power plant
tasks.source_note: The powers of the plant are an invented example in the size class of a large pressurised water plant. The heat of combustion of hard coal $24\,\tfrac{\text{MJ}}{\text{kg}}$ is a typical value.
tasks.text:
A Finnish nuclear power plant with a pressurised water reactor has an electric power of $1600\,\text{MW}$ when the thermal power of the reactor is $4300\,\text{MW}$. In the condenser the steam from the turbine condenses, and seawater is pumped in for cooling and warms up by $11\,\text{K}$. Assume that the plant runs at full power for the whole year.

- one fission of uranium-235 releases on average $200\,\text{MeV}$
- mass of a uranium-235 atom $235\,\text{u}$, $1\,\text{u} = 1.661 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$
- specific heat capacity of seawater $4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$
- $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$
- heat of combustion of hard coal $24\,\tfrac{\text{MJ}}{\text{kg}}$, efficiency of a coal power plant $40\,\%$
- assume that all the heat that does not become electricity goes to the seawater in the condenser

parts.text: How large is the efficiency of the plant, and how many fissions happen in the reactor per second?
hints: What part of the thermal power becomes electricity? How are the thermal power and the energy of one fission related when $n$ fissions happen per second?

The efficiency and the thermal power:
$$
\eta = \dfrac{P_\text{e}}{P_\text{th}}, \quad P_\text{th} = nE_\text{f}
$$

Convert the energy of a fission to joules: $200\,\text{MeV} = 2.00 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{eV}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. The thermal power is $4300\,\text{MW} = 4300 \cdot 10^{6}\,\dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{s}}$.

parts.text: How many kilograms of uranium-235 undergo fission in a year? How much mass is converted into energy in the same time?
hints: How many fissions happen in a year? What is the mass of one uranium-235 atom?
The mass of the uranium that undergoes fission is $m = n t\,m_\text{U}$. The mass converted into energy follows from $E = \Delta m\,c^2$, and the energy is $E = P_\text{th}\,t$.

Convert $m_\text{U} = 235\,\text{u} = 235 \cdot 1.661 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$ and $t = 1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$. Use the number of fissions per second $n$ from part a. Finally compare $\Delta m$ with the mass of the uranium that undergoes fission: what fraction of the mass is converted into energy?

criteria.text: Interprets that only about $0.09\,\%$ of the mass of the fissioned uranium is converted into energy; the rest remains as fission products and neutrons, because the mass number is conserved.

parts.text: How many kilograms of seawater must be pumped through the condenser per second?
hints: Where does the thermal power that does not become electricity end up? How large is it?

Energy is conserved, so the power transferred to the condenser heats the seawater:
$$
P_\text{th} - P_\text{e} = \dfrac{Q}{t}, \quad Q = c_\text{w}\,m\,\Delta T
$$
First calculate the power transferred to the condenser, $P_\text{th} - P_\text{e}$, and convert it to watts. Then solve the mass flow $\dfrac{m}{t}$ in symbols before substituting numbers.

criteria.text: Justifies that by conservation of energy the thermal power that does not become electricity, $P_\text{th} - P_\text{e} = 2700\,\text{MW}$, goes to the seawater in the condenser.

parts.text: How many tonnes of hard coal would a coal power plant burn in a year if it produced the same electrical energy?
hints: How much electrical energy does the plant produce in a year? How much thermal energy must a coal power plant burn to produce it?

The electrical energy is the power times the time, and the efficiency of the coal power plant links it to the heating value $H$ of the coal:
$$
E_\text{e} = P_\text{e}\,t, \quad \eta_\text{c} H m_\text{c} = E_\text{e}
$$

Convert $1600\,\text{MW} = 1600 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{W}$ and $24\,\dfrac{\text{MJ}}{\text{kg}} = 24 \cdot 10^{6}\,\dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}}$. Finally convert the answer from kilograms to tonnes, $1\,\text{t} = 1000\,\text{kg}$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{e} = P_\text{e} t$ and $E_\text{e} = \eta H m$, so $m = \dfrac{P_\text{e} t}{\eta H}$
About $5$ million tonnes, over three million times the mass of the fissioned uranium, because fission releases about $200\,\text{MeV}$ and burning a few electronvolts per reaction.

tasks.title: Did the fusion reactor produce more energy than it used?
tasks.source_note: Yle News 12 Dec 2022, article on the fusion experiment, in Finnish (https://yle.fi/a/3-12684377). Checked 16 Nov 2026. The energy the laser system took from the electricity grid, about $300\,\text{MJ}$, is a figure the laboratory gave in December 2022; it is not in the article.
tasks.text:
In December 2022 the news reported a breakthrough in fusion research. Open [the Yle News article on the fusion experiment](https://yle.fi/a/3-12684377) (12 Dec 2022, updated 13 Dec 2022; in Finnish, so use your browser's translation if you need it) and read all of it, including the correction note at the end.

According to the source (checked 16 Nov 2026) the two energies of the experiment were $3.15\,\text{MJ}$ and $2.05\,\text{MJ}$. The article compares the larger energy with bringing a few pots of water to the boil.

Further information:

- The specific heat capacity of water is $4.19\,\tfrac{\text{kJ}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$.
- According to the laboratory, the laser system took about $300\,\text{MJ}$ from the electricity grid for the shot. This figure is not in the article.
- A thermal power plant turns about a third of the energy it receives as heat into electricity.

parts.text: Find out from the source how the fusion reaction was produced. Which of the two energies in the source was released in the fusion reaction, and what does the other energy mean?
hints: Find the passage of the article that tells how the fusion was produced. Which two energy figures does the source mention, and what does each relate to?
Which energy is the input and which is the result? Think which one depends on the fusion reaction actually taking place.
Read the passage of the source that tells what the other energy includes or leaves out. Does it include the energy used to run the laser facility?

criteria.text: Tells from the source that the beams of huge lasers were focused on the point where the fuel was, and that in fusion nuclei join into heavier nuclei: helium forms and energy is released.

Interprets the energies: $3.15\,\text{MJ}$ was released in the fusion reaction, and $2.05\,\text{MJ}$ is the energy the lasers delivered to the fuel, which does not include the energy used to run the lasers.

parts.text: Calculate the ratio and the difference of the energies. What do they tell about the result of the experiment?
hints: Which of the energies is larger? How many times larger, and by how much?

The ratio and the difference of the energies, when $E_\text{f}$ is the energy released in the fusion and $E_\text{l}$ the energy the lasers delivered to the fuel:
$$
\dfrac{E_\text{f}}{E_\text{l}}, \quad \Delta E = E_\text{f} - E_\text{l}
$$
Both energies are in megajoules, so no conversion is needed and the ratio has no unit. Finally think about whose energy balance the result tells about.

criteria.detail: Fusion released about $1.5$ times the energy, that is $1.10\,\text{MJ}$ more than the lasers delivered to the fuel. The ratio is greater than $1$, which was the new result of the experiment.

parts.text: Check the article's comparison by calculation. How much water does the energy $3.15\,\text{MJ}$ heat from $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to the boiling point $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$? Does the comparison hold?
hints: Which equation gives the heat needed to warm water? Which quantity in it is unknown?
The heat needed to warm the water is $Q = c_\text{v}\,m\,\Delta T$. Solve the mass $m$ of the water from it.

Convert $3.15\,\text{MJ} = 3.15 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{J}$ and $4.19\,\dfrac{\text{kJ}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}} = 4190\,\dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$. The change in temperature is $\Delta T = 100\,{}^\circ\text{C} - 20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Finally compare the result with the article's estimate of “a few pots”.

criteria.detail: The comparison holds: about $9$ litres is a few pots, for example three pots of three litres.

parts.text: Explain why the result does not show that the whole experimental facility produced more energy than it used. Use the source and the electrical energy reported by the laboratory to justify your answer. Estimate also how much electrical energy the released energy would give with the efficiency of a thermal power plant.
hints: What does the energy figure $2.05\,\text{MJ}$ include? What energy did the laser facility take from the electrical grid?
Compare the energy released in the fusion, $3.15\,\text{MJ}$, with the energy taken from the grid, $300\,\text{MJ}$. Which system does each energy concern?
A thermal power plant turns about a third of the heat it receives into electricity. Calculate how much electricity would be obtained from $3.15\,\text{MJ}$ and compare it with $300\,\text{MJ}$.

criteria.text: Sets the system boundary: the comparison $3.15\,\text{MJ} > 2.05\,\text{MJ}$ concerns only the fuel. According to the source, the energy used to run the lasers is not included in the figure.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{3.15\,\text{MJ}}{300\,\text{MJ}} \approx 0.01$: fusion released about $1\,\%$ of the energy the facility took from the electricity grid.

criteria.text: States that the released energy was not turned into electricity. With the efficiency of a thermal power plant it would give about $1\,\text{MJ}$ of electricity, less than half a per cent of the energy taken from the grid.

parts.text: Another online outlet could give the same experiment this headline: “A fusion power plant already produces more energy than it uses.” The headline is invented for this problem. What should be made more precise in it? Use the article's own correction note as an example. Explain also why the result of the experiment does not violate conservation of energy.
hints: What does the headline suggest about a power plant and about the energy balance of the whole facility? Do both hold on the basis of the experiment?
Look at the article's correction note: what was changed and why? Which words or claim in the headline should be made more precise for the same reason?
Energy does not appear out of nothing. Which quantity of the nuclei changes in fusion, and which equation links it to energy?

criteria.text: Makes precise that this is a single laboratory experiment and not a power plant. A fitting reason is, for example, that no electricity was produced or that according to the source a fusion power plant connected to the grid is still decades away.

Makes precise that “more than it uses” holds only for the energy balance of the fuel, and connects this to the article's correction note: the headline and the text were changed so that the reader does not think the lasers' energy is included in the figure.
Explains that energy is conserved: the extra energy corresponds to the decrease in the mass of the nuclei in fusion, $E = \Delta m c^2$, and does not come from nothing.

tasks.title: A concrete wall next to a radiation source room
tasks.source_note: The situation and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text:
A concrete wall separates a corridor of an isotope laboratory from a room with a gamma radiation source. The figure shows the dose rate $\dot{H}$ of gamma radiation on the corridor side as a function of the thickness $d$ of the wall. The dose rate decreases exponentially: $\dot{H} = \dot{H}_0\,e^{-\mu d}$. Here $\dot{H}_0$ is the dose rate without the wall and $\mu$ is the attenuation coefficient of concrete.

- the thickness of the wall is $18\,\text{cm}$
- a person stays in the corridor behind the wall $1.5\,\text{h}$ per working day, and there are $220$ working days a year
- the person is not a radiation worker, so their annual dose may be at most $1.0\,\text{mSv}$
- the dose rate is constant, and other radiation sources are not taken into account

parts.text: Use the graph to determine the attenuation coefficient $\mu$ of concrete.
hints: Read from the graph the dose rate without the wall and one other point far from the first one. How is the exponential model solved for the unknown $\mu$?
The model is $\dot{H} = \dot{H}_0\,e^{-\mu d}$, and $\dot{H}_0$ is the dose rate at $d = 0$. Solve $\mu$ by taking the natural logarithm of both sides of the equation.

Calculate the ratio $\dot{H}_0 / \dot{H}$ for the point you chose before taking the logarithm. The thickness is in centimetres and the dose rates in the same unit, so $\mu$ gets the unit $1/\text{cm}$.

criteria.detail: Two points far apart are read from the graph, for example $(0\,\text{cm};\ 80\,\mu\text{Sv/h})$ and $(10\,\text{cm};\ 20\,\mu\text{Sv/h})$.

parts.text: What is the dose rate in the corridor behind the wall?
hints: Which model gives the dose rate as a function of the wall thickness? Which values do you already have?
Use the model $\dot{H} = \dot{H}_0\,e^{-\mu d}$, where $\dot{H}_0$ is the dose rate without the wall and $d = 18\,\text{cm}$.
Calculate the exponent $\mu d$ first: it has no unit. Use the attenuation coefficient of part a as accurately as possible, not the rounded value.

parts.text: What dose does the person receive in the corridor in a year? Is the maximum dose exceeded?
hints: How many hours a year does the person spend in the corridor? How are the dose rate, the time and the dose related?
The dose rate is constant, so the dose is the dose rate times the time spent: $H = \dot{H}\,t$.
The time spent is $t = 1.5\,\text{h} \cdot 220$. Convert the dose from microsieverts to millisieverts, $1\,\text{mSv} = 1000\,\mu\text{Sv}$, and compare it with the maximum dose $1.0\,\text{mSv}$.

criteria.detail: dose $H = \dot{H}\,t$ when the dose rate is constant, and the time spent in a year $t = 1.5\,\text{h} \cdot 220$.
Compares the dose with the maximum dose $1.0\,\text{mSv}$: the dose is about twice as large, so the limit is exceeded.

parts.text: How thick must the wall be at least so that the annual dose does not exceed the maximum dose? Also name one assumption of the model that may make the result too small, and its effect.
hints: How large may the dose rate in the corridor be at most, when the time spent in a year is known? How does the wall thickness follow from it?
The limit of the dose rate is $\dot{H}_\text{max} = \dfrac{H_\text{max}}{t}$. Write the condition $\dot{H}_0\,e^{-\mu d} = \dot{H}_\text{max}$ and solve $d$ from it.
Convert $1.0\,\text{mSv} = 1000\,\mu\text{Sv}$ so that the units match. Then think what the model leaves out and how it would change the result.

criteria.detail: Solves the thickness from the condition $\dot{H} \cdot t \le 1.0\,\text{mSv}$: $d = \dfrac{\ln(\dot{H}_0 / \dot{H}_\text{max})}{\mu}$.
$d \approx 24\,\text{cm}$, rounded up, because $23\,\text{cm}$ would still give too large a dose.

criteria.text: Names an assumption that may make the result too small (for example scattering is ignored, the source is stronger or the time spent is longer) and justifies its effect: a real wall should be made thicker than the result.

tasks.title: The recession of galaxies and the age of the universe
tasks.source_note: The situation and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text:
An astronomer has measured the recession velocity $v$ and the distance $d$ of nine galaxies. The figure shows the data points and a fitted line through the origin. According to Hubble's law $v = H_0\,d$, where $H_0$ is the Hubble constant.

- $1\,\text{Mpc} = 3.086 \cdot 10^{19}\,\text{km}$ and $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$
- the astronomer observes a new galaxy that recedes from us at the velocity $8400\,\text{km/s}$

parts.text: Use the graph to determine the Hubble constant $H_0$.
hints: Which property of the line in the graph is the Hubble constant? Through which point does the line pass?

According to Hubble's law $v = H_0\,d$, $H_0 = \dfrac{v}{d}$. With two points read on the line:
$$
H_0 = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{d_2 - d_1}
$$
Choose a grid point on the line whose values can be read accurately and which is far from the origin. Read both $v$ and $d$. Do not use a measured point that is not on the line.

criteria.detail: Two points far apart are read from the line: the origin and $(250\,\text{Mpc};\ 18\,000\,\text{km/s})$.
$v = H_0\,d$, so $H_0 = \dfrac{v}{d}$, the slope of the line.

parts.text: How far away is the new galaxy?
hints: Which law links the recession speed and the distance? Which result of part a do you need?
Hubble's law $v = H_0\,d$, from which $d = \dfrac{v}{H_0}$ is solved.
Use the Hubble constant of part a and the speed $8400\,\text{km/s}$. Check that the units $\text{km/s}$ cancel and $\text{Mpc}$ is left.

criteria.detail: $d \approx 120\,\text{Mpc}$, two significant figures like the velocity.

parts.text: Estimate how long ago the distances between the galaxies were zero, assuming that the distances have grown at the same rate all the time. Give the answer in years.
hints: If the distance has grown at the same rate all the time, how long does it take for the distance to grow from zero to its present value?

The time is the distance divided by the speed, and according to Hubble's law:
$$
t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{1}{H_0}
$$
Convert $H_0$ to the unit $1/\text{s}$: $1\,\text{Mpc} = 3.086 \cdot 10^{19}\,\text{km}$, so $\text{km}$ cancels. Finally convert the time to years, $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: If the distance $d$ of a galaxy has grown from zero at the constant velocity $v$, the time is $t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{1}{H_0}$.

parts.text: Explain why the observation that all distant galaxies recede from us does not mean that the Milky Way is the centre of the universe.
hints: What does the straightness of the line in the graph tell about how the speed depends on the distance? What would you observe if you looked from another galaxy?
Imagine a balloon with dots drawn on its surface, and blow air into it. How does any one dot see the other dots?
Do the galaxies move through space, or does space stretch between them? Is there a centre on the surface of the balloon from which the expansion starts?

criteria.text: Explains that according to the graph the velocity is directly proportional to the distance, and the same law would be observed from any galaxy: every galaxy sees the others receding from it.

Gives a correct picture of the expansion: space itself expands and the distances between all galaxies grow (no explosion from a point), for example with the balloon comparison, or justifies the absence of a centre in another equally valid way.

criteria.detail: Concludes that the expansion has no centre and the Milky Way has no special place, because the observation is the same everywhere.
